raw_case_text:
A 72-year-old woman with a recent diagnosis of type 1 autoimmune hepatitis was admitted to our hospital for a three-day history of lower abdominal pain associated with rectal bleeding.
In December 2011, the patient was admitted for the first time to our unit with marked fatigue and blood results suggestive of acute hepatitis (ALT = 1152 IU/L, AST 755 IU/L, total bilirubin 2.95 mg/dL, and directed bilirubin 2.13 mg/dL). Viral markers (HAV, HBV, HCV, CMV, and EBV) were negative, while ANA and ASMA were positive (1 : 320 with homogeneus pattern and 1 : 80, resp.). AMA and anti-LKM were negative.
A liver biopsy has been resulted compatible with a diagnosis of autoimmune hepatitis.
Prednisone was started at dose of 1 mg/Kg/die and azathioprine at a dose of 100 mg/die. After 10 days, the blood results were within the normal range, and the patient was symptoms free.
The steroid dose was gradually decreased. The patient felt well until February 2012 when she was readmitted for abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. At this time, she was on 0.5 mg/Kg/die of Prednisone and 100 mg/die of azathioprine. On admission to our unit, blood pressure was 150/90 mm Hg, pulse was 90 bpm, and temperature was 36.4 C. Her BMI was 25. No abuse of drugs was reported. Physical examination was normal. Laboratory values on admission were haemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, haematocrit 38%, MCV 94 fl, white cell count 10.130/cc, platelet count 202 000/cc, creatinine 0.69 mg/dL, total bilirubin 1.02 mg/dL, GGT 24 IU/L, AST 11 IU/L, ALT 36 IU/L, and LDH 458 IU/L; protein C reactive was 4 mg/dL, while procalcitonin and other inflammatory markers ware negative. Also blood cultures and stool cultures were negative. The coagulation tests like protein C, protein S, and antithrombin III, factor V Leiden mutation, and prothrombin 20210G/A mutation were all negative.
On the day after admission, the patient underwent colonoscopy (see Figure 1) which revealed severe active pancolitis (from rectal mucosa to all the colon), severe mucosal edema and erythema, multiple erosions, and rare ulcerations. An ultrasound showed thickening of the bowel wall.
The histological examination shows a modest and diffuse ischemic injury involving the entire colon. A mild hyalinization of lamina propria, a loss of superficial epithelium and ghost of crypts, with dilation and congestion of mucosal capillaries, have been seen (see Figure 2).
The histological examination, not compatible with a vascular injury, and the absence of signs of infection have allowed a diagnosis of drug-induced ischemic colitis secondary to drugs use.
Symptoms regressed after some day reducing steroid therapy (0.2 mg/Kg/die of Prednisone) and the patient did not require any blood transfusion.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 72-year-old woman with type 1 autoimmune hepatitis presented in February 2012 with a 3-day history of lower abdominal pain and rectal bleeding.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two months prior (December 2011), the patient presented with marked fatigue and acute hepatitis (ALT 1,152 IU/L, AST 755 IU/L, total bilirubin 2.95 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 2.13 mg/dL, ANA 1:320 homogeneous, ASMA 1:80, negative HAV/HBV/HCV/CMV/EBV/AMA/anti-LKM, and diagnostic liver biopsy), achieving biochemical and clinical remission within 10 days on prednisone (1 mg/kg/day) and azathioprine (100 mg/day). While maintained on tapered prednisone (0.5 mg/kg/day) and azathioprine (100 mg/day), she was readmitted in February 2012 with 3 days of lower abdominal pain and hematochezia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis (diagnosed December 2011 via serology and liver biopsy). No history of drug abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 3 days of lower abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. Home medications: prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day and azathioprine 100 mg/day.

objective.physical_examination: Blood pressure 150/90 mmHg, heart rate 90 bpm, temperature 36.4 °C, BMI 25 kg/m2; physical examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: February 2012 admission labs: hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, hematocrit 38%, MCV 94 fL, WBC 10,130/mm3, platelets 202,000/mm3, creatinine 0.69 mg/dL, total bilirubin 1.02 mg/dL, GGT 24 IU/L, AST 11 IU/L, ALT 36 IU/L, LDH 458 IU/L, CRP 4 mg/dL, negative procalcitonin, negative blood and stool cultures, and negative thrombophilia panel (protein C, protein S, antithrombin III, Factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A). (Prior Dec 2011 viral serologies for HAV, HBV, HCV, CMV, and EBV were negative.) Abdominal ultrasound showed bowel wall thickening.
objective.advanced_workup: Colonoscopy on hospital day 2 revealed severe active pancolitis extending from the rectum throughout the entire colon with severe mucosal edema, erythema, multiple erosions, and rare ulcerations. Colonic mucosal biopsies demonstrated diffuse modest ischemic injury across the entire colon characterized by mild lamina propria hyalinization, superficial epithelial loss, crypt ghosts, and mucosal capillary dilation and congestion without vasculitis or infectious cytopathic changes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Diagnosed with steroid/drug-induced ischemic pancolitis in a patient with type 1 autoimmune hepatitis (confirmed by characteristic ischemic colonic histology showing lamina propria hyalinization and ghost crypts without vascular thrombosis or infectious agents; viral infections including CMV and EBV, bacterial enterocolitis, and hereditary thrombophilias ruled out). Following reduction of oral prednisone dosage from 0.5 mg/kg/day to 0.2 mg/kg/day, abdominal pain and rectal bleeding resolved within a few days without requiring blood transfusion.
